claims.text: OCSA led the Sky Canada Project to review current practices surrounding public reporting of unidentified aerial phenomena in Canada, and published its report, 'Management of Public Reporting of Unidentified Aerial Phenomena in Canada', in June 2025 (59 pages, also issued as PDF).

claims.source: Sky Canada Project report, section A

sources.title: Report of the Sky Canada Project, Office of the Chief Science Advisor of Canada, June 2025

claims.text: OCSA states the project was spurred by increased public interest and by developments in other countries, particularly the United States, where formal procedures for addressing UAP sightings are in development.

sources.title: Report of the Sky Canada Project, Office of the Chief Science Advisor of Canada, June 2025

claims.text: The report recommends identifying the department responsible for managing public UAP data, establishing a dedicated service to collect testimonies, investigate cases and post its analyses publicly, and having Transport Canada, with NAV CANADA, encourage pilots, cabin crew and air traffic controllers to report UAP sightings without fear of stigmatisation.

OCSA records a published disclaimer that the project is not intended to collect first-hand data, not to make OCSA the main point of contact for reporting, and not to prove or disprove the existence of extraterrestrial life or visitors.

claims.source: Inference from the Sky Canada report
claims.text: A national science advisor publishing a finding that aircrew do not report because of stigma is an official admission that the observational record is systematically incomplete by social mechanism - which is the same mechanism a concealment programme would rely on and would not need to enforce. Reasoning: stated in the report's own recommendation to remove fear of stigmatisation.

connections.note: The Sky Canada report records that 'On June 1, 2024, AARO released its second report on 757 UAP reports from May 1, 2023, to June 1, 2024', of which '174 cases were resolved and found to be objects such as balloons, birds, unmanned aerial systems, satellites and aircraft', and cites AARO's Historical Record Report Volume I in its references. Its recommendation 13 directs the future Canadian lead organization to 'establish partnerships with international entities dedicated to UAPs, such as AARO and NASA (U.S.A.), GEIPAN (France), and SEFAA (Chile).'

desc: The Office of the Chief Science Advisor of Canada (OCSA) is the federal science-advice body that reports into the Government of Canada's science portfolio and advises the Prime Minister and the Minister of Innovation, Science and Industry. In 2022-2025 it ran the Sky Canada Project, a formal review of how public reports of unidentified aerial phenomena are handled in Canada, and on 30 June 2025 it published 'Management of Public Reporting of Unidentified Aerial Phenomena in Canada', a 59-page report of the project. The report is careful about its own limits - it explicitly states it is not intended to collect first-hand data, not to make OCSA the reporting point of contact, and not to prove or disprove extraterrestrial life or visitation - but it does something more useful for this board: it maps the actual Canadian reporting landscape, naming Transport Canada's CADORS occurrence system, the RCAF and Department of National Defence, the National Research Council's 1967-1990s collection role, and the RCMP, OPP and Sûreté du Québec as de facto intake points, and it finds the whole arrangement fragmented and gap-ridden. Its recommendations - identify the department that owns public UAP data, stand up a dedicated service that investigates and publishes its analyses, and have Transport Canada and NAV CANADA actively encourage aircrew and controllers to report without stigma - amount to a Western government stating on the record that stigma suppresses reporting and that transparency is the corrective. OCSA sits on this board as the clearest case of a G7 science authority treating UAP as a legitimate data-governance problem rather than as a subject to be denied.
